title: Cookie banners that do not cover the offer
metaTitle: Cookie banners that leave the offer clear
excerpt: Keep the cookie notice small, plain, and clear of the headline. The first thing a buyer reads should be the offer, not a consent bar.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper. The plain page of writing fits an article about a notice that should stay small and readable.
caption: The notice should be as plain as the sentence it must not cover. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should a cookie banner sit?
faqs.answer: Put it at the edge of the screen, usually along the bottom, and keep it short enough that the headline stays visible. It should not take the first screen, and it should not sit on top of the button that books a call. A buyer should understand the offer before they deal with the notice.

faqs.question: What should the banner say?
faqs.answer: Say that the site uses cookies, name the choice, and link to the privacy page for the detail. Two clear actions beat a wall of categories on first paint. If you need granular choices, put them one step away, in language a person can answer without a glossary.

faqs.question: Can a banner hurt the page even after someone dismisses it?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it shifts the layout when it appears or when it leaves. web.dev's threshold for a good Cumulative Layout Shift score is 0.1 or less. Reserve the space or overlay the bar in a way that does not push the headline. And do not show it again on every page of the same visit once the person has answered.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The cookie notice is a duty. It is not the introduction. Good cookie banner ux keeps the bar small, the language plain, and the headline uncovered. A buyer should meet the offer first. The consent question can wait at the edge of the screen.

If the first thing a stranger can read is a vendor's paragraph about categories, pixels, and legitimate interest, you have handed them the wrong page. They came to learn what you do. The banner can be answered in a glance. It should be written so a glance is enough.

## The first ten seconds belong to the offer

Nielsen Norman Group's account of page visits is the right clock for this. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. The first 10 seconds are when they decide whether your value is clear enough to stay. A banner that occupies that window spends the decision on storage policy.

Put the notice where the eye goes last, not first. A short bar along the bottom works on most marketing pages. The headline, the supporting line, and the primary action stay in view above it. If the bar is so tall that the action sits underneath it, the bar is the page.

Do not delay the banner so it slides in after they start to read. A late arrival is a jump. It covers the button at the moment they choose to tap. Show it with the first paint, in a reserved place, or overlay it so the text underneath does not move. Then leave it still.

The same rule applies on the second page of the visit. Once they have answered, remember the answer for the visit and longer if your policy allows. A banner that returns on every route trains people to swat at the corner of your site instead of reading it.

## Small, plain, and possible to finish

Write two actions a person can tell apart. "Accept" and "Reject" should look like peers if both are real choices. A bright accept button and a reject link in low-contrast type is a dark pattern, and serious buyers notice. You can prefer a default in the policy. You should not hide the other path.

Keep the first text to a sentence or two. Name that you use cookies, say they cover what the visitor needs to know at this step, and link to the privacy page. The privacy page is where the list lives. The banner is where the decision lives. Pasting the policy into the bar makes the decision harder and the offer invisible.

If the law or your counsel requires categories, open them on request. "Manage choices" can lead to a short panel: necessary, measurement, marketing. Each row gets a plain description of what it does on this site, not a vendor's boilerplate about "enhancing your experience." If you cannot explain a category in one line, you may not need that category.

Match the site's type, color, and buttons. A stock banner from a platform, in a new window or a typeface you do not use, feels like a different company interrupted yours. The notice can be legally serious and still look like it belongs. Plain is the brand move. Decoration is how the bar grows until it covers the work.

## What the bar must not cover

The headline. The primary action. The price, if price is how a buyer judges fit. Focus, when someone is moving with a keyboard. A banner that sticks to the bottom and hides the last link in the footer on a short phone is a permanent obstacle, not a one-time notice.

Test the shortest phone you support, in the browser's default text size, and again with a larger text size. Banners that fit a desktop mock often wrap to half the screen on a phone. If the offer is gone at that size, rewrite the banner before you rewrite the hero.

Do not pin a second bar above it. A newsletter strip plus a cookie bar plus a holiday announcement is three interruptions before the product. Pick the one you are required to show. Let the others wait until the person has seen the page, and even then, do not stack them.

Leave the page usable while the banner is up. Scrolling, reading, and the main link should work. A modal that dims the whole site and refuses to scroll is a wall. Use it only when you truly cannot proceed without a choice, and even then keep the wall short. Most marketing sites can let people read while the bar sits at the edge.

## Motion, shift, and the script that arrives late

web.dev sets a good Cumulative Layout Shift score at 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of loads. A banner injected after the headline has painted will push that headline down and can fail the threshold by itself. It also feels like the page flinched.

Load the notice with the page, in a region that already has its height, or take it out of the document flow so it overlays without pushing. When it closes, do not collapse the layout if that yanks the button out from under a finger. Overlay, or animate nothing and simply remove it.

Be careful with the script that renders the banner. If it is a large third-party tag, it can delay the largest content on the page and slow the first tap. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less for a good score. A consent tool that blocks the main thread has failed the visit before anyone answers it. Prefer a small, first-party bar you control. Bring in the heavier platform only if you have a real reason, and load it so the offer still paints.

Give the bar an accessible name, real buttons, and a focus order that reaches those buttons without a trap. When it closes, return focus to the page, not to the top of the document where the person loses their place. Esc can close a panel that was opened on purpose. It should not silently accept tracking.

## Match the promise on the privacy page

The banner and the privacy page have to agree. If the bar says measurement is optional, the page should say what measurement means here, in the same words. If rejecting non-essential cookies still leaves a stack of marketing tags running, the interface is a costume. Buyers who check will trust you less, and they are the buyers who read.

List the cookies you actually set. A young company often needs a session cookie, a preference for the banner itself, and maybe one measurement tool. That is a short list. It does not need the language of a global network. When you add a tool, update the page the same week. A stale list is how the banner starts to lie.

Say how long you keep the choice. Say how to change it later, in the footer, without hunting. "Cookie settings" in the footer is a quiet, sufficient path. A floating badge on every screen is another banner.

This is a design and engineering problem that sits next to counsel, not a substitute for it. The studio can make the notice readable, stable, and on-brand. The decision about what you must ask, in which region, belongs to someone who can advise you. Bring that answer to the build. Do not leave it as a default inside a plugin you have not read.

Region is a layout problem as well as a legal one. A visitor who does not need the bar should not get an empty gap where the bar would have been. Detect what you must show, then render that version with the space already accounted for. A bar that pops in only for some countries, and shoves the hero down when it does, is the shift bug with a flag on it.

Keep a record of the choice in a place your team can see. When someone writes in to say the site still tracked them after they refused, you want a clear answer, not a guess about which script loaded. The banner is the visible part. The tag list is the part that has to obey it.

## Review it like a first screen

Open the site in a private window so the choice is fresh. Before you scroll, say out loud what the company does. If you cannot, because the banner is the only readable text, the layout is wrong. Then answer the banner both ways, accept and reject, and confirm the page does not jump and the tags follow the answer you gave.

Check a keyboard pass and a phone pass. Check the privacy link. It should open in the same site, in the same type, not a PDF in a new window that looks like a vendor. The legal page can be plain. It should still be yours. That standard is the same one we use for the rest of the interface.

When you are ready for a site where the offer stays in front and the notices stay in their place, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The banner is a small piece of a page that has to be readable as a whole.

The same standard covers contrast, focus, names, and motion. [Accessibility on a marketing site](/blog/accessibility-on-a-marketing-site) is the next piece, because a banner that is merely small can still be impossible to use if the type is faint or the buttons have no names.
